title: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California (2020)
shortTitle: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California (2020)
summary: The rescission of DACA was arbitrary and capricious because the agency failed to consider retaining deferred action separately from benefits and failed to assess reliance interests, and post hoc reasons offered nine months later could not cure those defects.
notes:
Key line: "But Duke's memo offers no reason for terminating forbearance." (Roberts, C.J.)

Citation: 591 U.S. 1 (2020).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the Department of Homeland Security, its Acting Secretary and other federal officials, and in the companion cases the President and the Acting Secretary. The respondents were the Regents of the University of California, the State of California and other states, individual DACA recipients, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, and the plaintiffs in Batalla Vidal v. Wolf from the Eastern District of New York. The three consolidated cases were No. 18-587 from the Ninth Circuit and Nos. 18-588 and 18-589 on certiorari before judgment to the D.C. and Second Circuits.
sections.Material Facts: In June 2012 DHS issued the DACA memorandum allowing certain unauthorized aliens who arrived as children to apply for two year renewable forbearance from removal; recipients became eligible for work authorization and federal benefits, and about 700,000 people enrolled. In 2014 DHS expanded DACA and created DAPA for 4.3 million parents of citizens and lawful residents. Texas and 25 other states obtained a nationwide injunction against DAPA and the expansion; the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that DAPA conflicted with the Immigration and Nationality Act's definition of benefits eligibility while distinguishing forbearance, and the Supreme Court affirmed by an equally divided vote in 2016. In September 2017 Attorney General Sessions advised Acting Secretary Elaine Duke that DACA shared DAPA's legal defects, and the next day Duke rescinded DACA, ending new applications and allowing renewals only for recipients whose benefits expired within six months. In June 2018 Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen declined to disturb the rescission and added policy reasons.
sections.Procedural History: Plaintiffs sued in the Northern District of California, the Eastern District of New York and the District of Columbia, alleging that the rescission was arbitrary and capricious under the APA and violated equal protection. Each district court rejected the government's arguments that the decision was unreviewable and that the INA barred jurisdiction. The California and New York courts entered nationwide preliminary injunctions requiring DHS to continue renewals; the D.C. court granted partial summary judgment, stayed its order for ninety days to allow a fuller explanation, and then found Nielsen's memorandum inadequate. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the California injunction, 908 F.3d 476 (2018). The Supreme Court granted certiorari and certiorari before judgment, heard argument on November 12, 2019, and on June 18, 2020, affirmed the D.C. judgment, vacated in part and reversed in part the Ninth Circuit's judgment, and remanded all cases.
sections.Issue: Whether DHS's rescission of DACA was reviewable under the APA or was a nonenforcement decision committed to agency discretion under Heckler v. Chaney, and whether the INA's jurisdictional provisions barred review; whether the rescission was arbitrary and capricious, including whether the Court could consider Secretary Nielsen's later explanation and whether Acting Secretary Duke adequately considered retaining forbearance without benefits and the reliance interests of DACA recipients; and whether the plaintiffs plausibly alleged that the rescission was motivated by animus in violation of the equal protection guarantee of the Fifth Amendment.
sections.Holding: The Court held that the rescission was reviewable because DACA was not simply a nonenforcement policy but a program conferring affirmative relief and benefits, and that the INA provisions did not apply. It held that judicial review was limited to the grounds Duke invoked in September 2017; because Nielsen elected to elaborate on the original decision rather than take new action, her new reasons were impermissible post hoc rationalizations. It held the rescission arbitrary and capricious because Duke, bound only by the Attorney General's conclusion about benefits, failed to consider whether to retain forbearance, the centerpiece of the policy, and failed to consider whether there was legitimate reliance on DACA. A plurality concluded that the equal protection claim was not plausibly alleged.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts explained that the APA requires reasoned decisionmaking and that Michigan v. EPA limits review to the grounds the agency invoked. An agency whose reasons are found inadequate may elaborate on its original reasoning or deal with the problem afresh through new action, as Chenery and Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. v. LTV allow, but it may not offer new reasons for an old decision; the rule promotes accountability, guards against convenient litigating positions and permits orderly review. Turning to Duke's memorandum, the Court accepted that she was bound by the Attorney General's determination that DACA was illegal, but the Fifth Circuit opinion he relied on concerned eligibility for benefits and carefully distinguished the forbearance component. Removing benefits while continuing forbearance therefore remained within her discretion, yet her memo offered no reason for terminating forbearance. That repeated the error in State Farm, where a rationale supporting only part of a policy was treated as sufficient to rescind the whole. Duke also failed to address reliance, although Smiley v. Citibank requires an agency changing course to consider serious reliance interests; recipients had enrolled in degree programs, started careers, bought homes and married in reliance on DACA. DHS could have concluded that reliance interests were outweighed or considered accommodations such as a longer wind down, but it had to assess them first. On equal protection, the plurality found no plausible inference of discriminatory purpose.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: Regents applies State Farm to the unconsidered forbearance alternative and Fox to serious reliance interests.
topics.lrs-n-administrative-record: Nielsen’s distinct later reasons could not sustain Duke’s earlier rescission absent a new agency action.
topics.lrs-n-nonreviewability: The DACA program’s application process and associated benefits supported review rather than treatment as a simple nonenforcement policy.
topics.lrs-n-policy-change-reliance: Regents requires the agency to weigh reliance even though DACA disclaimed an entitlement to continuation.
topics.lrs-o-chenery-reasons: The Court refused to consider Secretary Nielsen's later-added reasons as a defense of Acting Secretary Duke's rescission because they were post hoc rationalizations rather than a new agency action.

learning.separateOpinions: Justices Ginsburg, Breyer and Kagan joined the opinion in full and Justice Sotomayor joined all but Part IV. Justice Sotomayor concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that the equal protection claim should have been allowed to proceed. Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Alito and Gorsuch, concurred in the judgment in part and dissented in part, arguing that DACA was unlawful from its inception so its rescission required no further explanation and the Court's decision created a perverse incentive for agencies never to correct unlawful programs. Justice Alito wrote separately to criticize the years of litigation blocking the rescission. Justice Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment in part and dissented in part, arguing that the Court should have considered the Nielsen memorandum and that it adequately addressed reliance interests.
